payload.throughline: Start from electron occupancy, then use energy, pairing, valence pattern, shells, and effective nuclear charge to predict observable atomic behavior.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: read the principal number, subshell label, and electron count from one configuration term.
Purpose: you will be able to construct and check bounded electron configurations rather than treating notation as an unstructured string.

The principal quantum number n labels a shell. Within the bounded configurations used here, an s subshell holds up to two electrons and a p subshell up to six. A superscript states occupancy, not charge.

Each orbital holds at most two electrons, and paired electrons in one orbital have opposite spin under Pauli exclusion. Count the atom or ion electrons first, then fill the supplied conventional order and verify the total.
Mental model — count, place, constrain, verify: determine electron number, place electrons in the bounded order, enforce capacities, and add superscripts to recover the starting count.
Think aloud: neutral oxygen has eight electrons. Filling 1s² and 2s² uses four; the remaining four enter 2p, giving 1s² 2s² 2p⁴. The superscripts sum to eight.
Worked atom: sodium has eleven electrons, so 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ uses ten and the final electron enters 3s¹.
Worked ion: Na⁺ has ten electrons after losing the 3s electron, so its bounded configuration ends at 2p⁶.
Guided practice: sum superscripts and match the total to a neutral atom.
Less help: detect an orbital-capacity or Pauli violation.
On your own: write a representative-atom configuration from electron count.
Boundary: a superscript greater than subshell capacity is invalid, and two same-spin electrons cannot share one orbital. This lesson does not ask for transition-metal exceptions.
Near exit: select the valid bounded configuration for a fresh neutral atom.
Changed-task exit: change the electron count by ion formation before selecting the configuration.
Repair atom configuration: sum superscripts, enforce s and p capacities, and compare the sum with atomic electron count.
Fresh re-entry: construct a different neutral p-block configuration.
Repair ion configuration: compute electrons after charge first; only then alter the outer occupancy.
Fresh re-entry: apply that electron-count rule to a different simple ion.
Recap from memory: define n, state s and p capacities, state Pauli exclusion, and explain why every configuration check ends by summing electrons.
Each failed configuration function receives one targeted cue and one untouched re-entry. A second miss returns control without exit credit.
Starting check: distinguish a ground state from an excited electronic state.
Purpose: you will be able to read discrete energy-level diagrams and select a different threshold model for photoelectron emission.

The ground state is the lowest available electronic energy; an excited state is higher. Absorption moves an electron upward when photon energy matches a permitted gap. Emission occurs on a downward transition and releases a photon with energy equal to the gap.

In the photoelectric effect, a photon must exceed a material threshold energy. Above threshold, increasing frequency increases maximum photoelectron kinetic energy; increasing intensity at fixed above-threshold frequency increases photon number and can increase emitted-electron count, not single-electron maximum energy.
Mental model — bound-level gap versus escape threshold: use discrete differences for spectral lines and photon energy minus threshold for photoelectrons.
Think aloud: a transition from 5 eV to 2 eV is downward, so it emits a 3 eV photon. I subtract final from initial only after identifying direction.
Worked absorption: a 2 eV-to-6 eV transition requires absorption of a 4 eV photon.
Worked photoelectric case: if the threshold is 3 eV and photons carry 5 eV, the maximum kinetic energy is 2 eV; brighter 5 eV light adds photons but does not raise that 2 eV maximum.
Guided practice: compute a downward transition gap.
Less help: match upward and downward arrows to absorption and emission.
On your own: connect a larger energy gap to photon frequency.
Boundary: line absorption requires a matching bound-state gap; photoelectric emission requires exceeding an escape threshold. Intensity and photon energy are not interchangeable.
Near exit: infer emitted photon energy and frequency ranking from a fresh level diagram.
Changed-task exit: switch models and predict the effect of raising light intensity below the photoelectric threshold.
Repair level transitions: identify initial and final states, take the positive energy difference, and label upward as absorption or downward as emission.
Fresh re-entry: apply that gap reasoning to a different pair of levels.
Repair threshold reasoning: compare energy per photon with threshold before considering photon count or intensity.
Fresh re-entry: use above-threshold frequency and a changed intensity in an untouched photoelectric case.
Recap from memory: define ground and excited states, state the absorption/emission directions, and distinguish threshold, frequency, and intensity in photoelectric behavior.
One model-specific cue and one untouched re-entry bound each exit function. A second miss returns control without exit credit.
Starting check: distinguish a singly occupied orbital from a paired orbital.
Purpose: you will be able to infer magnetic behavior from electron occupancy while avoiding claims unsupported by the supplied model.

A bounded species with one or more unpaired electrons is paramagnetic. A species with every electron paired is diamagnetic. The classification follows occupancy, not whether the atom is a metal or nonmetal.

An ion can change the number of unpaired electrons by adding or removing electrons. If the configuration or orbital occupancy is not supplied and cannot be constructed within scope, the honest conclusion is that classification is unresolved.
Mental model — scan for single arrows: one unpaired electron is sufficient for paramagnetism; zero unpaired electrons supports diamagnetism.
Think aloud: a p subshell diagram shows one paired orbital and two singly occupied orbitals. Because at least one electron is unpaired, I select paramagnetic without needing to compare pair counts.
Worked diamagnetic case: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ has only filled subshells, so all electrons are paired.
Worked paramagnetic case: 1s² 2s² 2p⁵ leaves one unpaired p electron in the bounded orbital diagram.
Guided practice: count unpaired electrons in an explicit orbital diagram.
Less help: classify a filled-shell configuration.
On your own: classify a partially filled p subshell from supplied occupancy.
Boundary: atomic mass, net charge sign, or metallic category alone does not decide pairing. Do not claim a magnetic class without occupancy evidence.
Near exit: classify a fresh explicit orbital occupancy.
Changed-task exit: infer how simple ion formation changes pairing before classifying the ion.
Repair occupancy classification: ignore paired orbitals after confirming them and search the entire diagram for any single electron.
Fresh re-entry: classify a different supplied subshell diagram.
Repair ion magnetism: update electron count and orbital occupancy first, then re-count unpaired electrons.
Fresh re-entry: apply that sequence to a different simple ion.
Recap from memory: define paramagnetic and diamagnetic in occupancy terms and state when the classification must remain unresolved.
One pairing-specific cue and one untouched re-entry bound each exit function. A second miss returns control without exit credit.
Starting check: identify a filled outer-shell pattern from supplied valence notation.
Purpose: you will be able to classify periodic families from electronic structure rather than memorizing isolated names.
Representative elements occupy the s and p blocks. Common bounded patterns include ns¹ for alkali metals, ns² for alkaline-earth metals, ns²np⁵ for halogens, and a filled outer shell for noble gases.

Transition elements occupy the d block and often show partially filled d subshell behavior. Metals dominate the left and center of the table; nonmetals cluster toward the upper right, with classification based on the supplied position and electronic structure.
Mental model — outer pattern, block, family: read the highest-n valence pattern, identify s, p, or d block, then select the bounded group classification.
Think aloud: an outer pattern ns²np⁵ is one electron short of a filled p shell. That is the halogen pattern, not a noble gas or alkaline-earth pattern.
Worked representative case: [core]4s¹ is an s-block ns¹ pattern and therefore an alkali-metal pattern.
Worked transition case: a highlighted central-table d-block element is classified as transition rather than representative even when an outer s subshell is also occupied.
Guided practice: map ns¹ to its group family.
Less help: distinguish halogen from noble-gas valence patterns.
On your own: classify an s-, p-, or d-block element from a provided pattern.
Boundary: the outer s occupancy alone does not make a d-block element representative. Hydrogen is not treated as an ordinary alkali metal solely from ns¹ in this bounded classification.
Near exit: identify a fresh representative family from valence structure.
Changed-task exit: use a provided block and periodic position to distinguish representative, transition, metal, and nonmetal labels.
Repair family classification: compare the highest-n s and p occupancies with the four named family patterns.
Fresh re-entry: classify a different outer-shell pattern.
Repair block classification: locate the differentiating subshell and table region before assigning representative or transition status.
Fresh re-entry: apply that block-first rule to a different highlighted position.
Recap from memory: state the four valence patterns and distinguish representative from transition elements and broad metal from nonmetal regions.
One classification cue and one untouched re-entry bound each exit function. A second miss returns control without exit credit.
Starting check: decide whether adding a principal shell tends to increase or decrease atomic radius.
Purpose: you will be able to explain periodic trends with shell count and effective nuclear charge rather than only recalling arrows.

Down a group, added principal shells generally increase atomic radius and lower first ionization energy. Across a period, increasing effective nuclear charge generally pulls valence electrons closer, decreasing radius and increasing ionization energy and electronegativity.

Electron affinity generally becomes more favorable across a period but has important exceptions, so use provided comparisons rather than a universal monotonic rule. Cations are smaller than their neutral atoms; anions are larger. Within an isoelectronic series, more protons pull the same electron count into a smaller radius.
Mental model — shells versus pull: added shells expand and shield; stronger effective nuclear attraction contracts and makes electron removal harder.

Think aloud: two isoelectronic ions have ten electrons, but one has twelve protons and the other eleven. The twelve-proton ion is smaller because the same electron cloud experiences stronger attraction.
Worked period comparison: moving right with the same principal shell generally increases effective nuclear charge, so radius decreases while ionization energy rises.
Worked ion comparison: Na⁺, Ne, and F⁻ have ten electrons; Na⁺ has the most protons and is smallest, while F⁻ has the fewest and is largest.
Guided practice: predict atomic-radius direction down a group.
Less help: predict ionization-energy direction across a period.
On your own: connect electronegativity to effective nuclear attraction.
Boundary: trend arrows are broad patterns, not exception-free laws. Do not rank electron affinity from a generic arrow when the prompt supplies an exception or lacks a bounded comparison.
Near exit: compare two neutral atoms using one shell-count or effective-charge difference.
Changed-task exit: switch to ions and rank an isoelectronic set by proton count.
Repair atomic trends: ask first whether shell count changes; if not, compare effective nuclear attraction across the period.
Fresh re-entry: apply that choice to a different neutral-atom comparison.
Repair ion size: compare electron counts, identify isoelectronic species, then use proton count; otherwise compare atom with its cation or anion.
Fresh re-entry: rank a different ion pair using the same bounded sequence.
Recap from memory: explain radius, ionization energy, electronegativity, electron-affinity caution, cation and anion size, and isoelectronic ranking.
One trend-specific cue and one untouched re-entry bound each exit function. A second miss returns control without exit credit.
